passage: On the first morning of the new year, Yuki knocked on five doors of the Leeds block and left small plates of mochi, saying happy new year to each. Bilal, across the landing, returned the plate with samosas a week later. On a frosty morning Bilal's car would not start before an important appointment, and Yuki drove there without being asked. Months on, Yuki's Saturday music carried through the wall. Bilal sent a text: "Small request, could the bass go down a little tonight?" Yuki felt no sting, just a smile, and turned it down at once. Nobody needed a meeting or a letter. The greetings and plates had already made room for an easy word.

qa.q: What did Yuki leave on five doors at New Year?
qa.a: Yuki left small plates of mochi.

qa.q: What did Yuki feel on reading Bilal's text, and why?
qa.a: Relaxed and willing, because earlier kindness had built trust and the polite message did not feel like an attack.

qa.q: Why did the noise problem end so easily?
qa.a: Greetings, shared food and a lift had built goodwill, so both spoke kindly and the music went down.

qa.q: How might Bilal have felt when Yuki drove on the frosty morning?
qa.a: Relieved and grateful, which made it easier to ask politely later.

grounding: A young adult greets neighbours, shares festival food and helps in need, and goodwill makes a later conflict easy to settle.

passage: On Diwali evening the community centre hall smelled of ghee. Anjali set a tray of besan laddoos on the long table and said good evening to each person coming in, even the two who never nodded on the stairs. Tejas, from the flat opposite, took one and said, "I never thanked you for carrying my shopping last month." Anjali laughed. "You can thank me by joining the phone list for emergencies." Tejas wrote a name and number on the sign-up sheet. Weeks later, when the shared water tank overflowed at midnight, that list brought five neighbours in ten minutes, and a small squabble about whose turn it was to mop was over in a shrug.

qa.q: How long did it take five neighbours to arrive when the tank overflowed?
qa.a: Five neighbours arrived in ten minutes.

qa.q: Why did Anjali greet even the two who never nodded, and what did Anjali want?
qa.a: To include everyone and build trust, hoping small warmth would open a connection.

qa.q: What small step by Anjali prepared the lane for the midnight overflow?
qa.a: Asking neighbours to join a phone list for emergencies.

qa.q: How does Tejas see Anjali?
qa.a: As a kind neighbour worth thanking; Tejas mentions the shopping and signs the list.

grounding: A young adult offers sweets and help to neighbours, and stored goodwill makes emergencies and small conflicts easier.

passage:
Hi Vikas,
Remember how you laughed at me for knocking on every door in the building the week I moved in, with a plate of kaju katli? Well. Last Tuesday at 2 a.m. the pipe under my sink burst. Water everywhere, me in a towel, panicking. I called Mrs D'Souza downstairs because I had her number from the Diwali plate. She came up in her nightie with a torch and knew exactly where the main valve was. Her son brought buckets. By three we were drinking tea on her sofa.
And then, the funny part: two days later, the man on the fourth floor, the one who fights with everyone about parking, came to ask if the water had leaked into his flat. Because I knew him a little, we sorted it in five minutes.
So, I win.
Pallavi

qa.q: At what time did the pipe burst?
qa.a: At 2 a.m. last Tuesday.

qa.q: How did Pallavi feel when the pipe burst, and what shows it?
qa.a: Pallavi was panicking, standing in a towel with water everywhere, and then relieved when Mrs D'Souza came up with a torch.

qa.q: What habit paid off for Pallavi, and how?
qa.a: Greeting neighbours with sweets when moving in meant Pallavi had a number to call at 2 a.m. and some goodwill when the fourth-floor man came to complain.

qa.q: How might the fourth-floor man have reacted if he did not know Pallavi at all?
qa.a: He might have come ready for a fight, as he does about parking, and the leak could have become a long quarrel instead of a five-minute chat.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult whose greetings and festival sweets built goodwill that helped in an emergency and made a conflict easy to resolve.

passage: Madhav, you keep asking why I bother with the neighbours. Let me, Yamini, tell you about last monsoon. When I moved into the old building in Chennai, I did the dull stuff. Said vanakkam on the stairs. At Pongal I took a little steel box of sweet pongal to every flat, even to the grumpy man on the first floor, Mr Iyer. He barely said thanks. Then in July I slipped on the wet stairs and twisted my ankle, alone. Guess who heard me? Mr Iyer. He called an auto, came with me to the clinic, and waited two hours. A month later there was a fight about the water tank timings. Normally that meeting would have been a war. Mr Iyer stood up and said, "Let's hear the young lady." It was sorted in twenty minutes. That's why I bother.

qa.q: What did Yamini take to every flat at Pongal?
qa.a: A little steel box of sweet pongal.

qa.q: What might Yamini have been feeling while lying on the stairs with a twisted ankle?
qa.a: Yamini was probably frightened and helpless, being hurt and alone, and then grateful and surprised when Mr Iyer came.

qa.q: What would you advise Madhav, based on Yamini's story?
qa.a: Madhav could try small, regular gestures, like greetings and festival sweets, even with grumpy neighbours, since goodwill builds slowly and helps in emergencies.

qa.q: How might Mr Iyer have felt about Yamini after the Pongal box?
qa.a: He may have felt noticed and quietly touched, even if he barely said thanks, which is perhaps why he helped and later backed her at the meeting.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult whose greetings, festival sweets and neighbourliness built goodwill that brought help in an emergency and eased a dispute.

passage: I'm Uma, from the flat opposite, so I watched Neelam's first year in our building. I can't say what was in her head, only what she did. She learnt everyone's name within a fortnight, even the watchman's children. On Eid she carried a tray of sheer khurma down the corridor. At Diwali she lit a diya outside the Mehtas' door when they were away. When old Mrs Pinto had a fall, Neelam was the one on the phone to the ambulance, holding her hand on the landing. Then, in March, the new car-parking lines were painted and her car ended up half in Mr Rao's space. Mr Rao is famous for his temper. I waited for shouting. Instead he came to her door, laughed, and said, "We'll repaint that line together on Sunday." They did.

qa.q: What did Neelam carry down the corridor on Eid?
qa.a: A tray of sheer khurma.

qa.q: What was Uma feeling when Neelam's car ended up in Mr Rao's space?
qa.a: Uma was anxious and braced for shouting, because Mr Rao is known for his temper.

qa.q: What made the parking problem easy to settle?
qa.a: Neelam's months of kindness had built trust, so Mr Rao treated the mistake as something to fix together rather than a fight.

qa.q: How did Mr Rao see Neelam when her car was in his space?
qa.a: He saw her as a good neighbour who had helped others, not as an intruder, so he felt relaxed enough to laugh and offer to repaint the line together.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who greets neighbours, shares festival food and helps in emergencies, building goodwill that eases a later conflict.

passage:
Diwali week. Irawati, new to the building, carried a plate of kaju katli to every flat on her floor, including the Deshmukhs, who had never once nodded back in the lift. Jahnavi Deshmukh took the plate at the door without a smile.
A Tuesday in January. At midnight the Deshmukhs' door banged open: Jahnavi's father had collapsed in the bathroom. Irawati, still awake, ran over, called the ambulance and held the lift while the paramedics came up. She sat with Jahnavi in the hospital corridor till four.
March. A leak from Irawati's flat stained the Deshmukhs' ceiling. Irawati braced for a fight when Jahnavi rang the bell. Instead Jahnavi said, "The plumber can come Thursday. Split the bill?" They settled it in five minutes, over tea, and Jahnavi returned the Diwali plate she had kept since October.

qa.q: What sweet did Irawati carry to every flat?
qa.a: She carried a plate of kaju katli.

qa.q: What did Irawati feel when Jahnavi rang the bell in March?
qa.a: Irawati felt anxious, bracing for a fight over the leak.

qa.q: Why was the March problem so easy to solve?
qa.a: The goodwill Irawati had built, from Diwali sweets to sitting with Jahnavi at the hospital, made Jahnavi ready to cooperate rather than fight.

qa.q: What might Jahnavi have felt sitting with Irawati in the hospital corridor?
qa.a: Jahnavi was likely frightened for her father and deeply grateful not to be alone, which changed how she saw her neighbour.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who shares festival sweets and helps in an emergency, building goodwill that makes a later conflict easy to resolve.
